Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I Queer are the ways of a man I know: He comes and stands In a careworn craze, And looks at the sands And the seaward haze With moveless hands And face and gaze, Then turns to go... And what does he see when he gazes so? II They say he sees as an instant thing More clear than to-day, A sweet soft scene That once was in play By that briny green; Yes, notes alway Warm, real, and keen, What his back years bring— A phantom of his own figuring. III Of this vision of his they might say more: Not only there Does he see this sight, But everywhere In his brain–day, night, As if on the air It were drawn rose bright– Yea, far from that shore Does he carry this vision of heretofore: IV A ghost-girl-rider. And though, toil-tried, He withers daily, Time touches her not, But she still rides gaily In his rapt thought On that shagged and shaly Atlantic spot, And as when first eyed Draws rein and sings to the swing of the tide.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Queer, And, With

outputs.L1:
I

Strange are the ways of a man I know:  
He comes and stands in a careworn daze,  
And looks at the sands and the seaward haze  
With motionless hands and fixed face and gaze,  
Then turns to go...  
And what does he see when he gazes so?

II

They say he sees, in an instant,  
More clearly than to-day,  
A sweet, soft scene  
That once was in play  
Beside that briny green;  
Yes, he recalls always,  
Warm, real, and keen,  
What his past years bring—  
A phantom of his own imagining.

III

Of this vision of his they might say more:  
Not only there  
Does he see this sight,  
But everywhere  
In his mind—by day, by night—  
As if upon the air  
It were drawn, rose-bright;  
Yes, far from that shore  
He carries this vision of heretofore:

IV

A ghostly girl-rider. And though, toil-worn,  
He withers daily,  
Time touches her not;  
She still rides gaily  
In his rapt thought  
On that rugged, shaly Atlantic spot,  
And, as when first seen,  
Draws rein and sings to the swing of the tide.
outputs.L2:
I

Strange are the habits of a man I know:  
he arrives and stops there,  
lost in a worn, troubled daze.  
He stares across the sand  
and into the mist over the sea,  
his hands utterly still,  
his face and eyes fixed.  
Then he turns away to leave...  
But what is it that appears to him  
as he looks so intently?

II

People say that, in a single moment,  
he beholds something clearer than the present day:  
a gentle, lovely scene  
that once unfolded  
beside that salty green water.  
Always, they say, he senses it—  
warm, vivid, and sharp—  
brought back by the years behind him:  
a specter shaped by his own memory.

III

More could be said about this vision of his:  
it is not only in that place  
that he sees it.  
He sees it everywhere,  
inside his mind—by day, by night—  
as though it had been sketched in rosy brightness  
upon the very air.  
Yes, even far away from that shore,  
he carries with him this image from long ago.

IV

It is the apparition of a girl on horseback.  
And though he, worn down by labor,  
grows weaker day by day,  
time does not alter her.  
She still rides joyfully  
within his absorbed imagination  
over that rough, stony Atlantic place;  
and just as when he first saw her,  
she checks her horse and sings  
in rhythm with the moving tide.
outputs.L3:
A careworn man stands again and again by the shore, gazing in silence at the sands and the sea haze. To anyone passing by, he appears to be looking out over the Atlantic, watching the mist drift above the water and the tide draw its pale line along the beach. Yet there is something in his stillness that suggests his eyes are fixed on more than the present scene before him.

Those who know him believe he is not truly seeing the shore as it is now. Instead, they think he is looking into a vivid memory from his past, one so powerful that it has never faded. The ocean, the sand, and the dim veil of salt air seem to open a doorway in his mind, returning him to a moment that remains more real to him than the world around him.

This vision follows him everywhere. It is with him in the brightness of day and in the darkness of night, at the shore and far from it. No matter where he goes, the image rises before him with the same clarity: a ghostly young woman riding along the Atlantic sands, full of motion and life, as if untouched by time.

The man himself grows older. His face becomes more worn, his body more weary, and the years leave their marks upon him. But the girl in his memory never changes. She remains forever young, joyful, and radiant, riding beside the sea as though she belongs to a world beyond aging, sorrow, and loss.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a deeply melancholy portrait of a careworn man whose mind is fixed not on the present, but on a powerful memory from the past. As he stands gazing out toward the sea, the speaker repeatedly wonders what the man sees in the shifting coastal landscape. The waves, shore, horizon, and sea-wind create an atmosphere of distance and haunting uncertainty, as though the outer scene reflects the man’s inner life. His fixed stare suggests that he is not merely looking at the water, but looking through it, beyond the present moment, into some earlier time that continues to possess him.

The poem’s repeated speculation builds a sense of mystery around his vision. At first, it is unclear whether he sees something real, something imagined, or something remembered. The coastal imagery helps intensify this ambiguity: the sea is vast, restless, and difficult to read, much like memory itself. It can conceal as much as it reveals. The man’s worn appearance contrasts with the vividness of whatever holds his attention, suggesting that time has marked his body but has not weakened the emotional force of the past.

The central revelation is that he carries within him an unaging image of a “ghost-girl-rider” from long ago. This figure seems to belong to memory, desire, and loss all at once. She remains untouched by time, preserved in the form in which he first knew or imagined her. While the man has grown older and more burdened, the girl in his mind has not changed. She survives as a ghostly presence, both absent and intensely alive.

Through this contrast, the poem shows how memory can outlast the conditions of ordinary life. The rememberer may decline, but the remembered image can remain bright, fixed, and emotionally overwhelming. The man’s fixation is therefore both beautiful and tragic: beautiful because it testifies to the enduring power of feeling, and tragic because it traps him in a past that cannot return. The poem ultimately suggests that memory is not always a fading echo. Sometimes it remains vivid and untouched, haunting the present with the force of what has been lost.
outputs.L5:
**Queer, And, With**

Queer is not only a word for identity; it is also a way of seeing, questioning, and imagining. It makes room for lives that do not fit neatly into categories, for love that refuses narrow definitions, and for people who create themselves beyond expectation.

And is a small word, but it holds great power. It connects rather than separates. It says we can be many things at once: queer and joyful, queer and uncertain, queer and proud, queer and still becoming. It reminds us that identity does not have to be simple to be real.

With is a word of community. No one should have to stand alone in their truth. To live with others, to grow with support, to speak with courage, and to love with openness is part of building a kinder world.

Together, **Queer, And, With** becomes a message of inclusion. It celebrates complexity, connection, and belonging. It says there is space for every story, every body, every voice, and every way of being.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic four-part poem in the style of Thomas Hardy about an old man staring at the sea and remembering a ghostly young woman on horseback.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. The Cliff**

He stood where the thrift in the wind was thin,  
And the gulls went crying by,  
An old man, bowed as a thorn is bowed  
When winters have shorn it dry.  

Below him the waters shouldered on,  
Grey-green, with a graveward gleam,  
And every wave that fell and fled  
Seemed part of a former dream.  

No hand at his sleeve, no voice at his ear,  
No foot on the chalk behind—  
Only the sea’s old argument  
With the ruinous edge of the wind.  


**II. The Rider Remembered**

Yet once, ere the fields grew strange to him,  
And his blood took time to flow,  
She came by the lane on a coal-black mare,  
In the dusk of years ago.  

Her hat was dark, and her cheek was pale,  
And her hair had the sunset’s fire;  
She looked but once from the saddle down,  
And woke in him long desire.  

The hoof-beats rang on the hollow road,  
Then dwindled across the lea;  
But ever since, when the day falls wan,  
They return from the edge of the sea.  


**III. The Apparition**

For there, where the foam on the shingle dies  
And the blown sand veils the grass,  
He fancied her riding the tideline still,  
A shape no storm could pass.  

The mare made never a mark on shore,  
No breath from her nostrils came;  
The woman’s eyes were the eyes he knew,  
Yet emptied of their name.  

“O why,” he whispered, “through all these years  
Do you keep that silent pace?”  
But the surf replied with a thousand tongues,  
And none had her voice or face.  


**IV. The Sea’s Reply**

The sun went out like a taper spent,  
The headlands hardened black;  
The old man turned from the whitening waves,  
But his heart went always back.  

Back to the road and the ringing hoofs,  
Back to the glance once thrown,  
Back to the life he had never lived,  
And the love he had never known.  

And far below, in the darkening tide,  
Where the last pale waters gleamed,  
The ghostly rider passed and passed—  
Or so the old man dreamed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Victorian-era lyric poem with Roman numeral sections, archaic diction, coastal imagery, and the theme of memory haunting a worn, aging man.
counterfactuals.output:
I.

Beside the wrack-strewn, whitening shore  
An old man walketh, bent and grey;  
The gulls cry out for evermore,  
The tide steals all but grief away.  

His cloak is salt, his beard is blown  
Like thistle-down in winter’s breath;  
He treadeth where the moon hath shone  
On shells as pale and cold as death.  

And ever, from the foam’s dim verge,  
There comes a voice he cannot flee—  
Half lullaby and half a dirge,  
“Remember me—remember me.”  


II.

O long ago! when blood was warm,  
And dawn rose rosy from the main,  
He loved a maid with eyes of storm,  
With lips like rain on window-pane.  

She bound his scarf with fingers white,  
She watched his vessel lift and veer;  
The harbour-lamps, that mournful night,  
Were stars fallen low to tremble near.  

“Return,” she said; “though years divide,  
Though tempests drive thee far from lea.”  
He laughed, and kissed her by the tide—  
Now echoes answer: “Where is she?”  


III.

The cliffs are worn, the church-bells fail,  
The sea-mist dims the village panes;  
Yet in his heart one ghostly sail  
Still glimmers through the mortal rains.  

At dusk he sees her on the strand,  
Her shawl blown backward like a wing;  
She lifts no face, she gives no hand,  
But heareth he her dead lips sing.  

“Thou wast so fair; thou wast so proud;  
Thou wouldst not heed the waning sea.”  
The waves draw in their sable shroud,  
And whisper, “Memory—memory.”  


IV.

Now leaneth he where sea-grass shakes  
Above the graves of drowned and dear;  
The night-wind through the headstones wakes  
Old sorrows from their sepulchre.  

His eyes, once bright with voyaging,  
Are lanterns spent in fog and rain;  
Yet still the vanished summers cling  
Like seaweed to a broken chain.  

O Lord of tide, and cloud, and foam,  
Give rest to hearts that late repent;  
For memory hath no earthly home,  
Yet haunteth every tenement.  

And when at last the ebb is low,  
And all his weary pulses flee,  
May that lost voice he loved below  
Call softly from eternity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a Hardy-like poem set on an Atlantic shore, where a careworn man sees a vivid phantom from his past whenever he gazes out to sea.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Face Beyond the Breakers**

Upon the gaunt Atlantic strand,  
Where gulls wheel grey and grasses lean,  
A man with weather-wearied hand  
Stands watching that unquiet scene.

The tide comes in with ancient sound,  
The shingle shifts, the sea-winds cry;  
And every wave that laps the ground  
Seems charged with some dim bygone sky.

For when he looks beyond the foam,  
Past mast and cloud and westward star,  
There rises, as from youth and home,  
A face he has not seen afar—

No mist-made blur, no dream half-done,  
But clear as dawn on window-glass:  
Her eyes, once lit with April sun,  
Her hair the brown of meadow-grass.

She stands where green seas lift and fall,  
Unwet, unwaning, near yet fled;  
And though the storm-birds wheel and call,  
He hears the words she never said.

“O had I known,” his lips begin—  
The breakers strike the rocks below;  
“O had I turned from pride and sin—”  
The wild tide answers, “Long ago.”

Again he stares: she smiles as then,  
Before the years grew hard and strange;  
Before the hearts of women, men,  
Were bartered into grief and change.

He sees the lane, the gate, the rain,  
The dusk that took her shape away;  
The letter kept, the needless pain,  
The silence deeper than the bay.

Yet with each surge her image gleams,  
As if the ocean’s furthest plain  
Had gathered all his ruined dreams  
To give them back—and take again.

So there he stands when evenings pale,  
A bent black form beside the sea,  
While westward drives the lonely sail  
And night comes on remorsefully.

And still, where moon and waters meet,  
She shines—too dear, too late, too fair;  
The phantom youth could not entreat,  
The age-worn heart can only bear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a rhymed poem about a man who returns to a beach and is haunted by the vision of a girl rider unchanged by time.
counterfactuals.output:
He came where gulls were crying thin,  
Where tides erased the tracks of men,  
And felt the old years drawing in  
Like waves that break, withdraw, again.  

The dunes were bowed, the inn was gone,  
The pier lay black beneath the foam;  
Yet still the red sun lingered on  
The shore that once had seemed like home.  

Then down the strand, through silver spray,  
A rider flashed beside the sea—  
A girl as bright as yesterday,  
As wild as wind, as young as she.  

Her loosened hair was dusk and flame,  
Her laughter rang above the tide;  
The horse she rode was still the same,  
With moonlight running at its side.  

He called her name—his voice was drowned  
By surf that thundered cold and wide;  
She turned, but time made not a sound,  
Nor cast one shadow where she’d ride.  

No wrinkle touched her fearless face,  
No sorrow dimmed her shining eyes;  
She kept forever that lost grace  
The heart remembers, age denies.  

Past him she flew, a ghost of gold,  
Beyond the reach of hand or breath;  
He stood upon the shore grown old,  
And watched his youth outride his death.  

Now when the evening tides return  
And stars like broken shells appear,  
He walks the beach where memories burn  
And hears her hoofbeats drawing near.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a somber English poem with sea haze, sands, memory, and a ghostly horsewoman, using stanza divisions marked I–IV and an old-fashioned poetic voice.
counterfactuals.output:
I

Upon the shore where sea-haze dimly lies,  
And muffled breakers toil beneath the moon,  
The pallid sands, outspread to mournful skies,  
Remember footsteps vanished all too soon.  
No gull makes cry; the wind hath lost its breath,  
And all the night is hearkening unto death.  

II

There memory walks, with garments wet and gray,  
And gathers shells where once glad voices passed;  
She names the names the tide hath worn away,  
And weeps to find their echoes fading fast.  
O bitter strand, O foam’s unfaithful scroll,  
What hand shall write again the perished soul?  

III

Then, through the haze, where hollow waters gleam,  
There rides a horsewoman, spectral, wan, and lone;  
Her steed’s pale mane is tangled like a dream,  
His hoofs strike sparks from sands as cold as stone.  
No bridle rings, no living heart draws nigh—  
She passeth by, with sorrow in her eye.  

IV

And evermore, when midnight veils the deep,  
And ancient griefs arise from drowned years,  
She keeps her vigil where the sea-winds weep,  
A shade of love, a messenger of tears.  
Ah, who can tell what vow the waters keep,  
Or why the dead ride forth when mortals sleep?
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
